main_chase_cards.name: Pikachu [Non-glossy]
main_chase_cards.why: Pikachu is the teach-me face of the pair, and this print matters because the How-to-Play route corrects the earlier CoroCoro glossy illustrator credit to Keiji Kinebuchi while moving onto regular stock.

main_chase_cards.name: Jigglypuff [Non-glossy]
main_chase_cards.why: Jigglypuff is the friendly second voice: soft, readable, and perfect for a rule-learning book that needed the TCG to feel less intimidating.

key_artists.name: Keiji Kinebuchi
key_artists.why: Kinebuchi matters here because the pair is about making the game legible. His credit sits directly on the corrected Pikachu print and the Jigglypuff companion, turning artist metadata into an identification rail rather than a decoration.

claims.text: The local release and selected early-1996 promo snapshot place the Easily Understand How to Play Pokemon Cards promo pair on November 30, 1996.
The selected snapshot lists two non-glossy Easily Understand How to Play Pokemon Cards entries: Pikachu [Non-glossy] and Jigglypuff [Non-glossy].

PokeBoon classifies both How-to-Play cards as 1996 Book / Unopened promos, and Heritage describes the object as the original Easily Understand How to Play Pokemon Cards magazine/book made to teach the rules of the TCG with two unnumbered promotional cards.
Bulbapedia distinguishes the October 15, 1996 CoroCoro glossy Pikachu/Jigglypuff pair from the November 30, 1996 Easily Understand How to Play Pokemon Cards non-glossy / regular-stock pair.
The local rows and PokeBoon card pages credit both How-to-Play Pikachu and Jigglypuff to Keiji Kinebuchi.
Bulbapedia says the How-to-Play Pikachu print updates the illustrator to the correct Keiji Kinebuchi after the earlier glossy CoroCoro print incorrectly credited Ken Sugimori.

The local release records Pikachu as a bounded manual provider-path row and Jigglypuff as a parent source-pinned row; manual provider-path rows are useful references, not parent aggregate decrypted rows or physical-card proof.
This source slice matters because it shows the TCG teaching itself: two friendly mascot-weight cards included with a rule-learning book so the new game could become playable, not merely collectible.

Agents should preserve November 30 1996 How-to-Play book route, non-glossy / regular-stock identity, Keiji Kinebuchi correction, Pikachu manual provider-path caveat, Jigglypuff row lineage, CoroCoro glossy non-equivalence, English Wizards promo non-equivalence, and Latest Edition Diglett/Dugtrio non-equivalence before accepting a match.

narrative.human_title: How-to-Play promos: the cards that taught the card game
narrative.why_it_matters: This pair feels gentle, but it is quietly one of the most important shapes in early Pokemon card culture. The booster made the game collectible; the How-to-Play book made it teachable. Pikachu and Jigglypuff are not trophies here. They are companions at the table, regular-stock reprints that say: you can learn this. The Pikachu credit correction is not trivia either; it is the paper trail of the apparatus correcting itself while the new game was still learning how to be explained.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: This Pikachu is not only early. It is corrective: the How-to-Play print updates the illustrator credit and turns a glossy magazine invitation into a regular-stock teaching-card object.

The local row, PokeBoon page, and Bulbapedia release note credit the How-to-Play Pikachu print to Keiji Kinebuchi.
Bulbapedia says this How-to-Play print uses regular card stock and corrects the earlier glossy CoroCoro print's Ken Sugimori illustrator miscredit to Keiji Kinebuchi.
This Pikachu matters because it is a teaching-card version of the mascot: a friendly entry point into the rules and a visible correction in the early paper trail.

Special identification must keep How-to-Play Pikachu row 003 separate from CoroCoro glossy Pikachu row 001, English Wizards Promo Pikachu 1, Toyota Pikachu, Intro Pack Pikachu, and later Pikachu promo memories.

narrative.why_it_matters: This is Pikachu as a classroom hand. The earlier glossy magazine print invited kids into the card world; this regular-stock How-to-Play print helped them understand what to do once they got there. The corrected Keiji Kinebuchi credit makes it feel even more alive: the apparatus is still young enough to fix its own labels.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Jigglypuff is the soft companion card in the pair: less market-loud than Pikachu, but crucial to proving the book route because the pair belongs together.

claims.text: The local catalog anchors Jigglypuff as How-to-Play source row 004.
The card is identified here as Jigglypuff / プリン / Purin.
The local row and PokeBoon card page credit How-to-Play Jigglypuff to Keiji Kinebuchi.

Bulbapedia says Jigglypuff was first available as a glossy CoroCoro insert on October 15, 1996 and later reprinted in Easily Understand How to Play Pokemon Cards on regular card stock on November 30, 1996.
Jigglypuff matters because it makes the teaching object feel friendly: a soft companion to Pikachu in a book built to make the new TCG readable.
Special identification must keep How-to-Play Jigglypuff row 004 separate from CoroCoro glossy Jigglypuff row 002, English Wizards Promo Jigglypuff 7, and later Jigglypuff promo memories.

narrative.why_it_matters: Jigglypuff is the quieter half of the book pair, and that quietness is exactly the point. The How-to-Play object needed the card game to feel approachable. Pikachu could pull your eye; Jigglypuff could soften the room. Together they make the TCG less like a rules sheet and more like something a kid might actually sit down with.
